author: polariscampus
text:
You can learn to code in a classroom. But can you build something when you have 24 hours, a team, a problem statement, and no idea if your idea is even going to work? 👀

That’s when Hackathons come into picture. They force you to build instead of just learning, figure things out instead of waiting for answers, and work with people who think differently from you. That kind of learning is hard to recreate inside a classroom - and it’s exactly why hackathons belong in a new-age curriculum.

And this one was BIG. 1,400+ participants joining us ON CAMPUS with Polaris students from Years 1, 2 and 3 getting right into the action 🎮 

Alongside the hackathon, students also got to attend workshops with @hiteshchoudharyofficial and mentors from AWS, getting hands-on with the tools, ideas and technology behind what they were building. There were also opportunities to take things a step further with direct interview rounds.

author.name: silviamogas.onchain in Dubai 🇦🇪
author.description: Capital Markets On Chain | Blockchain Marketing Boutique @bmbweb3 〰️ Entrepreneur, Creator & Speaker 〰️ (views are my own)

text:
Spent a few days last week at #VibeCon hosted by @Replit in #NewYork, and I left thinking less about what AI can build and more about what we should build with it.
The event mixed product, AI and creativity in a way that felt different. Builders weren't just talking about speed and agents. They were talking about taste, meaning, emotion and intention. And two panels captured that shift perfectly.

Creativity, Taste and Meaning in the Age of AI, with Michele Catasta and Meaghan Choi from @AnthropicAI 
The idea that stayed with me:
"Taste is not polish. Taste is discernment."
Because when almost anything can be built, the real value moves from execution to judgment. Taste is not the final visual layer. It starts much earlier: the problem you choose, the user you understand, the features you remove, the things you decide not to build at all. Building is getting easier. 
Choosing well is getting harder.

Everyone's a creative. Now what?, the closing conversation between Amjad Masad and spi

author: polariscampus
text:
What is the strongest tangible proof of coding competence in real-world scenarios?

Open Source it is. Which is strongly engraved into the culture of Polaris.

This year, 18 Polaris students became part of that culture through Google Summer of Code 2026.

And they’re not just contributing locally. They’re now working across open-source ecosystems spanning 9 countries, contributing to real-world systems in:
- cybersecurity
- healthcare & genomics
- developer infrastructure
- ⁠geospatial systems
- ⁠programming languages

Working alongside experienced mentors, building systems used by developers and organizations across the world.

But behind every selection is a completely different story.
While some students started with utmost clarity, some rebuilt from scratch after setbacks. Some learned by breaking things, fixing them, and trying again.
What connects all of them is simple:
They showed up consistently.
